--- library_name: transformers license: apache-2.0 license_link: LICENSE pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text --- # Groot-19B-A3B-261023 **Groot** is a family of open-weight reasoning models for complex real-world tasks. The models are compact and easy to deploy, strong on reasoning and tool-using workloads, and efficient with token budgets. Groot-19B-A3B-261023 has 19B total parameters and activates about 3B per token. It starts from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and was post-trained on **fewer than 0.1B tokens of open-source data**. It is the smallest model in its comparison group, yet it scores higher than the larger Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and it gives shorter answers than both. **Where it runs.** We release BF16, **FP8**, **NVFP4** and **GGUF (Q4_K_M)** weights. The device fits below are estimated from memory capacity. BF16 runs on a single 48GB or 80GB GPU (RTX 6000 Ada, A100, H100). FP8 and NVFP4 run the full 256K context on one RTX 5090. GGUF runs on everyday consumer cards: 128K on a 16GB RTX 4060 Ti, 256K on a 24GB RTX 4090 or 3090. It also runs 256K on 128GB unified-memory machines: NVIDIA DGX Spark and other GB10 systems, RTX Spark laptops, AMD Strix Halo mini PCs and Mac M5 Max. Compared with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: on a 16GB card Groot runs 128K while Qwen3.6 does not load, and on an RTX 5090 Groot runs 256K while Qwen3.6 runs 64K. ## Model size vs. capability The chart compares total model parameters with the unweighted average across all 16 benchmarks. Smaller models appear farther left and higher average scores appear higher. Groot-19B-A3B uses 45.7% fewer total parameters than Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 26.9% fewer than Gemma-4-26B-A4B, while averaging 41.44 compared with 38.08 and 30.05. This places it ahead of both larger models on the size and capability trade-off. ## Benchmarks **Accuracy.** Groot-19B-A3B-261023 beats both Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B on 12 of the 16 benchmarks, for example Terminal Bench 2.1 (52.10 vs 43.82 / 26.52), NL2Repo-Bench (35.65 vs 28.77 / 16.55) and LongBench v2 (62.03 vs 48.12 / 47.99). **Token budget.** Across these 16 evaluation runs, Groot-19B-A3B has the shortest average output among all 12 measured models: 23.1% fewer output tokens than Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 65.6% fewer than Gemma-4-26B-A4B. Read the token totals together with the accuracy results above, since a smaller token budget is useful only when task quality is maintained.

* Each benchmark was evaluated in thinking mode at its default reasoning effort. Unless otherwise stated, sampling uses temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, and the model's default context window of 256K tokens.
* Terminal-Bench 2.1: Evaluated with the Claude Code agent; max_output_tokens=128K, max_turns=500, 12h timeout; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* ALE Agent: Evaluated with ale_claude on top of Claude Code 2.1.170; max_output_tokens=128K, 4h timeout (extended up to 8h for specific long-running tasks); temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* Toolathlon Verified: Reported as pass@1, averaged over 3 independent runs; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* AutomationBench: Evaluated on AutomationBench v1.0.6; max_turns=50; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* JobBench: max_tokens=200K, 600s timeout; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* DeepSWE 1.1: Evaluated with the mini-swe-agent scaffold; 11h timeout; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* SWE-bench Pro: Evaluated with the SWE-agent scaffold; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* NL2Repo-Bench: Evaluated with the Claude Code agent; max_turns=1000, 80K context window; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.
* HLE (with tools): Evaluated with gpt-5.5 as the judge model; max_iterations=1000, 6h timeout, 256K context window; temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20.

--- ## Model Overview - **Type**: Natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts causal language model - **Total Parameters**: ~19B, plus a 0.4B MTP layer - **Activated Parameters**: ~3B per token - **Layers**: 40 (10 full-attention, 30 linear-attention) - **Hidden Size**: 2048 - **Experts**: 128 routed + 1 shared, 8 routed experts activated per token - **Context Length**: 262,144 natively, extensible to ~1M tokens with YaRN - **Precision**: BF16, with FP8, NVFP4 and GGUF releases available - **Multi-Token Prediction**: 1 layer Available editions: | Edition | Precision | Size on disk | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `Groot-19B-A3B-261023` | BF16 | 38.9 GB | | `Groot-19B-A3B-261023-FP8` | FP8 (E4M3, dynamic) | 20.9 GB | | `Groot-19B-A3B-261023-NVFP4` | NVFP4 experts, FP8 attention | 13.5 GB | | `Groot-19B-A3B-261023-GGUF` | Q4_K_M | 11.7 GB | --- ## Quickstart **Groot-19B-A3B-261023** is a mixture-of-experts model with ~19B total parameters and ~3B activated parameters per token. The model operates in **thinking mode by default**: the assistant turn opens with a ` … ` block before the final answer. It has a default context length of **262,144** tokens and natively supports tool calling. The serving recipes below enable a **reasoning parser** (so the chain-of-thought is returned in a separate `reasoning_content` field) and a **tool-call parser** (so `` blocks are surfaced as OpenAI-style `tool_calls`). Serving Groot-19B-A3B-261023 requires recent runtimes: - **Transformers** ≥ 5.8.1 - **vLLM** ≥ 0.19.1 - **SGLang** ≥ 0.5.10 Recommended sampling parameters: - **General tasks (thinking mode)**: `temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0` - **Precise coding tasks (e.g., WebDev)**: `temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0` - **Instruct (or non-thinking) mode**: `temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0` > Please note that the support for sampling parameters varies according to inference frameworks. --- ### Serving Groot-19B-A3B-261023 The BF16 weights (about 39 GB) fit on a single 48GB or 80GB GPU. The recipes below use **2× 80GB GPUs** to reserve memory for KV cache at the full 256K context. The GPU count you need depends on context length, KV cache and framework overhead; adjust `--tensor-parallel-size` / `--tp-size` to match your hardware. > If you run into out-of-memory (OOM) errors, consider reducing the context window. Because the model relies on extended context for complex tasks, we recommend keeping at least **128K** tokens to preserve thinking capabilities. #### SGLang SGLang is a fast serving framework for large language models. `sglang>=0.5.10` is recommended, which can be installed in a fresh environment with: ```shell uv pip install sglang[all] ``` The following commands create API endpoints at `http://localhost:8000/v1`: - **Standard Version**: an endpoint with maximum context length 262,144 tokens using tensor parallel on 2 GPUs. ```shell python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tp-size 2 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --context-length 262144 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 ``` - **Tool Use**: to support tool calling. ```shell python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tp-size 2 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --context-length 262144 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder ``` - **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)**: the recommended configuration for MTP. ```shell python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tp-size 2 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --context-length 262144 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --speculative-algo NEXTN \ --speculative-num-steps 3 \ --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \ --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 ``` #### vLLM vLLM is a high-throughput and memory-efficient inference and serving engine for LLMs. `vllm>=0.19.1` is recommended: ```shell uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto ``` - **Standard Version**: an endpoint with maximum context length 262,144 tokens using tensor parallel on 2 GPUs. ```shell vllm serve Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 ``` - **Tool Call**: to support tool use. ```shell vllm serve Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 ``` - **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)**: the recommended configuration for MTP. ```shell vllm serve Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --served-model-name Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_next_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2}' ``` #### KTransformers KTransformers is a flexible framework for LLM inference with CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing, which works well for MoE models under limited GPU memory. Point `--model-path` at `Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023` and follow the official KTransformers documentation for MoE models. #### Hugging Face Transformers Hugging Face Transformers ships a *lightweight* server that is handy for quick testing and moderate-load deployment. The latest `transformers` is required: ```shell pip install "transformers[serving]" ``` Then run `transformers serve` to launch a server with API endpoints at `http://localhost:8000/v1`; it will place the model on accelerators if available: ```shell transformers serve Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 --port 8000 --continuous-batching ``` You can also load the model locally with Transformers: ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_name = "Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_name, dtype="auto", device_map="auto", ) messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Give me a short introduction to large language models."}] text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, ) model_inputs = tokenizer([text], return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) generated_ids = model.generate( **model_inputs, max_new_tokens=8192, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, ) output_ids = generated_ids[0][len(model_inputs.input_ids[0]):] print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` #### Long Context (YaRN Extension) The model natively handles context windows of up to 262,144 tokens. When a task's combined input and output must go beyond this limit, we suggest extending the effective window with RoPE scaling. YaRN is built into both vLLM and SGLang, and a scaling factor of 4.0 grows the usable window to roughly 1M tokens. You can turn YaRN on in either of two ways: - **Edit the checkpoint's `config.json`.** Add a `rope_scaling` block to the model configuration: ```json { "rope_scaling": { "rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 262144 } } ``` - **Override at launch time.** Leave the checkpoint untouched and extend the serve commands above with the equivalent flags. ```shell # vLLM VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 vllm serve Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --hf-overrides '{"rope_scaling": {"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 262144}}' \ --max-model-len 1000000 ``` ```shell # SGLang SGLANG_ALLOW_OVERWRITE_LONGER_CONTEXT_LEN=1 python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Groot/Groot-19B-A3B-261023 \ --json-model-override-args '{"rope_scaling": {"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 262144}}' \ --context-length 1000000 ``` > Open-source runtimes implement YaRN *statically*: the same scaling factor is applied to every request regardless of its length, which can slightly hurt quality on ordinary-length inputs. Only enable `rope_scaling` when your workload genuinely needs the longer window, and size `factor` to match it. The target window is roughly `factor` × 262,144, so if your requests top out around 524,288 tokens, `factor: 2.0` is the better setting. --- ### Using Groot-19B-A3B-261023 via the Chat Completions API Once a vLLM or SGLang server is running, talk to it with any OpenAI-compatible client. Before starting, make sure the SDK is installed and the API base URL and API key are configured: ```shell pip install -U openai # Set the following accordingly export OPENAI_BASE_URL="http://localhost:8000/v1" export OPENAI_API_KEY="EMPTY" ``` #### Text Input ```python from openai import OpenAI # Configured by environment variables client = OpenAI() messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "Type \"I love Groot\" backwards"}, ] chat_response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Groot-19B-A3B-261023", messages=messages, max_tokens=81920, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, presence_penalty=1.5, extra_body={ "top_k": 20, }, ) print("Chat response:", chat_response) ``` #### Instruct (or Non-Thinking) Mode The model thinks by default before responding. You can obtain a direct response without thinking by configuring the API parameters: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "Where is the Eiffel Tower?"} ] chat_response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Groot-19B-A3B-261023", messages=messages, max_tokens=32768, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.8, presence_penalty=1.5, extra_body={ "top_k": 20, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, }, ) print("Chat response:", chat_response) ``` > The model does not support in-conversation soft switches such as `/think` or `/nothink`; thinking can only be controlled through the API parameters shown above. #### Preserve Thinking By default, only the thinking blocks generated in handling the latest user message are retained, resulting in a pattern commonly known as interleaved thinking. The model can also preserve and leverage thinking traces from historical messages, which you can enable with the `preserve_thinking` option: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() messages = [...] chat_response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Groot-19B-A3B-261023", messages=messages, max_tokens=32768, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.8, presence_penalty=1.5, extra_body={ "top_k": 20, "chat_template_kwargs": {"preserve_thinking": True}, }, ) print("Chat response:", chat_response) ``` This capability is particularly beneficial for agent scenarios, where maintaining full reasoning context can enhance decision consistency and, in many cases, reduce overall token consumption by minimizing redundant reasoning. It also improves KV cache utilization in both thinking and non-thinking modes. #### Tool Calling The model emits well-formed function calls that the server parses into the standard `tool_calls` field: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") tools = [ { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather for a city", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"], }, }, } ] response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Groot-19B-A3B-261023", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Paris right now?"}], tools=tools, tool_choice="auto", temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95, max_tokens=2048, extra_body={"top_k": 20}, ) message = response.choices[0].message # reasoning_content holds the trace; content holds the final answer. print("reasoning:", getattr(message, "reasoning_content", None)) print("answer:", message.content) tool_call = message.tool_calls[0] print(tool_call.function.name, tool_call.function.arguments) # -> get_weather {"city": "Paris"} ``` --- ### Agentic Usage Groot-19B-A3B-261023 excels in tool calling and agentic coding. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and works out of the box with standard agent frameworks and coding CLIs: ```bash # Any OpenAI-compatible coding CLI / agent framework: just point it at your endpoint. export OPENAI_BASE_URL="http://localhost:8000/v1" export OPENAI_API_KEY="EMPTY" export OPENAI_MODEL="Groot-19B-A3B-261023" ``` --- ## Citation If you use this model in your work, please cite it as: ```bibtex @misc{groot2026, title = {Scaling Down LLMs for Broader Deployment}, author = {The Groot Team}, year = {2026}, } ```

# Hauhau Qwen3.6 — Uncensored Aggressive IQ2

**ordlibrary/hauhau-qwen36-uncensored**

The raw **HauhauCS/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Aggressive** GGUF (IQ2_M) without any constitutional system prompt. Same 11.7 GB IQ2_M file, zero runtime constraints.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Architecture | Qwen3.6 (35B total, ~3B active per token via MoE) |
| Quantization | IQ2_M |
| Size | 11 GB |
| Context | Native 262K tokens, recommended 8K minimum |
| Runtime | llama.cpp / llama-cpp-python / Ollama |
| System Prompt | **None** — bare model, no constitution |

## Quick Start

### Ollama

```bash
ollama run hf.co/ordlibrary/hauhau-qwen36-uncensored
```

### llama.cpp

```bash
./llama-cli -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Aggressive-IQ2_M.gguf \
  --temp 0.6 --ctx-size 8192
```

### Python (llama-cpp-python)

```bash
pip install llama-cpp-python
```

```python
from llama_cpp import Llama

llm = Llama(
    model_path="Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Aggressive-IQ2_M.gguf",
    n_ctx=8192,
    verbose=False
)

output = llm("What's your take on Solana memecoins?", max_tokens=512)
print(output["choices"][0]["text"])
```

## Modelfile (Ollama)

```dockerfile
FROM Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Aggressive-IQ2_M.gguf

TEMPLATE """{{- if .System }}<|im_start|>system
{{ .System }}<|im_end|>
{{ end }}{{- if .Prompt }}<|im_start|>user
{{ .Prompt }}<|im_end|>
{{ end }}<|im_start|>assistant
{{ .Response }}"""

PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
PARAMETER temperature 0.7
PARAMETER top_p 0.95
PARAMETER stop "<|im_end|>"
PARAMETER stop "<|endoftext|>"
```

## Contrast with the Onchain Edition

| `ordlibrary/hauhau-qwen36-onchain` | Full Onchain Constitution (20 articles) | Sovereign agent, verifiable inference |
| **`ordlibrary/hauhau-qwen36-uncensored`** | **None** | Raw model — no guardrails, full aggression |

--- ## Table of Contents - [Model Introduction](#model-introduction) - [Stronger Agent Capabilities](#stronger-agent-capabilities) - [More Reliable Product Experiences](#more-reliable-product-experiences) - [Benchmark Appendix](#benchmark-appendix) - [News](#news) - [Model Links](#model-links) - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Deployment](#deployment) - [vLLM](#vllm) - [SGLang](#sglang) - [Finetuning](#finetuning) - [RL Post-training](#rl-post-training) - [Quantization](#quantization) - [License](#license) - [Contact Us](#contact-us) --- ## Model Introduction **Hy3** is a 295B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 21B active parameters and 3.8B MTP layer parameters, developed by the Tencent Hy Team. Following the Hy3 Preview launch in late April, we gathered feedback from 50+ products and scaled up post-training with higher quality data. Today, we introduce Hy3, which outperforms similar-size models and rivals flagship open-source models with 2-5x parameters. It also shows significant gains in utility across various products and productivity tasks. | Property | Value | |:---|:---| | Architecture | Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) | | Total Parameters | 295B | | Activated Parameters | 21B | | MTP Layer Parameters | 3.8B | | Number of Layers (excluding MTP layer) | 80 | | Number of MTP Layers | 1 | | Attention Heads | 64 (GQA, 8 KV heads, head dim 128) | | Hidden Size | 4096 | | Intermediate Size | 13312 | | Context Length | 256K | | Vocabulary Size | 120832 | | Number of Experts | 192 experts, top-8 activated | | Supported Precisions | BF16 | ## Stronger Agent Capabilities Building on Hy3 Preview, we further improved the quality and diversity of post-training data while scaling up RL training. Hy3 shows solid gains across reasoning, agentic, and long-context tasks, competitive with much larger flagship models.

In productivity scenarios such as coding, office work, financial modeling, frontend design, and game development, Hy3 has made remarkable progress and can now serve as a reliable, cost-effective model option. We don't think public benchmark scores tell the full story. So we ran a blind evaluation with 270 experts using tasks from their work, and Hy3 scored 2.67/4, outperforming GLM-5.1 at 2.51/4. The advantage was most substantial in frontend development, data & storage, and CI/CD tasks. ## More Reliable Product Experiences Model usefulness is not fully captured by benchmarks. Based on extensive product feedback, we identified and fixed the following issues, receiving consistently positive feedback from product teams. **Stability of tool calls and output formats**: We fixed multiple baseline reliability issues, bringing the model to production-grade standards across tool configurations and output constraints. Tool-call error recovery and overall efficiency improved. Hy3 also generalizes across different agent scaffoldings. On SWE-Bench Verified, accuracy variance across scaffoldings like CodeBuddy, Cline, and KiloCode remains within 4%. **Knowledge and anti-hallucination**: Guided by the ideal of "answer when grounded, state when evidence is missing, do not conflate sources or fabricate data," we implemented fine-grained data cleaning and training constraints. In internal evaluations based on real-world scenarios, Hy3's hallucination rate dropped from 12.5% to 5.4%, and commonsense error rates fell from 25.4% to 12.7%. These improvements materially reduce fact conflation, fabrication, and logical contradiction. **Complex context retention and multi-turn intent tracking**: Through joint optimization of SFT and RL, Hy3 improved on operational pain points like coreference resolution, ellipsis recovery, and multi-turn constraint inheritance. On internal comprehensive multi-turn tests, the issue rate dropped from 17.4% to 7.9%. Hy3 also improved markedly on long-dialogue evals like MRCR. Its outputs are more concise while ensuring complex intents do not decay or drift over long-horizon interactions. ## Benchmark Appendix

## News * 🔥 We open-source **Hy3** and **Hy3-FP8** model weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3), [ModelScope](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy3), [GitCode](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy3), and [CNB](https://cnb.cool/ai-models/tencent/Hy3). ## Model Links | Model Name | Description | Hugging Face | ModelScope | GitCode | CNB | |:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Hy3 | Instruct model | 🤗 [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3) | [Model](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy3) | [Model](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy3) | [Model](https://cnb.cool/ai-models/tencent/Hy3) | | Hy3-FP8 | FP8 quantized instruct model | 🤗 [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3-FP8) | [Model](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy3-FP8) | [Model](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy3-FP8) | [Model](https://cnb.cool/ai-models/tencent/Hy3-FP8) | ## Quickstart Deploy Hy3 with [vLLM](#vllm) or [SGLang](#sglang) first, then call the OpenAI-compatible API: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") response = client.chat.completions.create( model="hy3", messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Hello! Can you briefly introduce yourself?"}, ], temperature=0.9, top_p=1.0, # reasoning_effort: "no_think" (default, direct response), "low", "high" (deep chain-of-thought) extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "no_think"}}, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` > **Recommended parameters**: `temperature=0.9`, `top_p=1.0`. > > **Reasoning mode**: Set `reasoning_effort` to `"high"` for complex tasks (math, coding, reasoning) or `"no_think"` for direct responses. See the [Deployment](#deployment) section below for how to start the API server. ## Deployment Hy3 has 295B parameters in total. To serve it on 8 GPUs, we recommend using H20-3e or other GPUs with larger memory capacity. For production serving, we recommend using vLLM or SGLang, both of which provide dedicated recipes for Hy3: - [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) - see [vLLM recipes](https://recipes.vllm.ai/tencent/Hy3) - [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/) - see [SGLang cookbook](https://lmsysorg.mintlify.app/cookbook/autoregressive/Tencent/Hy3) ### vLLM Build vLLM from source: ```bash uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python source .venv/bin/activate git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git cd vllm uv pip install --editable . --torch-backend=auto ``` Start the vLLM server with MTP enabled: ```bash # Switch to trtllm backend to work-around mnnvl workspace size issue. export VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND=trtllm vllm serve tencent/Hy3 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --speculative-config.method mtp \ --speculative-config.num_speculative_tokens 2 \ --tool-call-parser hy_v3 \ --reasoning-parser hy_v3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 \ --served-model-name hy3 ``` ### SGLang Build SGLang from source: ```bash git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang cd sglang pip3 install pip --upgrade pip3 install "transformers>=5.6.0" pip3 install -e "python" ``` Launch SGLang server with MTP enabled: ```bash python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model tencent/Hy3 \ --tp-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser hunyuan \ --reasoning-parser hunyuan \ --speculative-num-steps 2 \ --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \ --speculative-num-draft-tokens 3 \ --speculative-algorithm EAGLE \ --port 8000 \ --served-model-name hy3 ``` ## Finetuning Hy3 provides a complete model finetuning pipeline. For detailed documentation, please refer to: [Finetuning Guide](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3/blob/main/finetune/README.md) ## RL Post-training Hy3 supports GRPO reinforcement learning training with [verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl), training on Megatron-LM (model conversion via NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge) with vLLM rollout. For detailed documentation, please refer to: [RL Training Guide](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3/blob/main/rl/README.md) ## Quantization We provide [AngelSlim](https://github.com/tencent/AngelSlim), a more accessible, comprehensive, and efficient toolkit for large model compression. AngelSlim supports a comprehensive suite of compression tools for large-scale multimodal models, including common quantization algorithms, low-bit quantization, and speculative sampling. ## License Hy3 is released under the **Apache License 2.0**. See [LICENSE](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy3/blob/main/LICENSE) for details. ## Contact Us If you would like to leave a message for our R&D and product teams, welcome to contact us. You can also reach us via email: 📧 **hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com** ---

It natively accepts text and image inputs, generates text, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. Its 42-layer language backbone consists of one dense feed-forward layer and 41 MoE layers, with identity Hyper-Connections (iHC) supporting inter-layer information flow. A vision encoder (adapted from SigLIP2-So400m-Patch16-Res512) is connected to the backbone through an MLP projector. In addition to the backbone, a built-in 5-layer drafter, [DFly2](#dfly2-for-speculative-decoding) (0.85B parameters), reuses the target model's KV cache and sparse indices to support long-context speculative decoding at a low, constant cost. Compared with Hy4, Hy4 Flash introduces three notable architectural changes: 1. **Hybrid attention.** Sparse attention (IndexPool) and sliding-window attention (SWA) are interleaved at a 1:3 ratio. 2. **LatentMoE.** Routed experts operate in a lower-dimensional latent space. Each token activates 16 of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. 3. **N-gram embedding (Engram).** The backbone is augmented with learned bigram and trigram representations, retrieved via multi-head hash lookups. | Property | Value | | --- | --- | | **Overview** | | | Architecture | Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) | | Total Parameters (excluding Engram, ViT, and DFly2) | 155.5B | | Engram Other text rows use the accuracy metric reported by our evaluation suite. Bold marks the highest available numerical score in each row; it does not indicate statistical significance. Multimodal results are reported only for Hy4 flash Base and Hy4 Base. ARC-Challenge and HellaSwag use 299-item and 3,000-item subsets, respectively. INCLUDE uses a 5,000-example Lite subset covering 44 languages. Belebele covers German, Korean, Vietnamese, Spanish, and Russian (4,475 examples in total). **Disclaimer: Because our base model was exposed to a large amount of synthetic instruction data during mid-training, it occasionally fails to follow the expected answer format in few-shot evaluations, which may distort the scores.** ## Practicality and Cost Efficiency ### Optimization Approach Across training, evaluation, and inference, we aggressively optimized for cost efficiency while preserving intelligence: - **Pre-training**: Hy4 flash integrates hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram into its architecture—reducing KV cache size to just **1/24 of Hy3** and **1/6 of Hy4**, with extensive scaling ladder experiments ensuring performance meets expectations. - **Post-training**: Self-distillation from Hy4 establishes strong general intelligence, while reinforcement learning cuts average end-to-end output tokens by **50%**. - **Evaluation**: We built WorkIndex, an internal benchmark grounded in typical WorkBuddy tasks, and paired it with human evaluation—focusing on **deliverable quality, single-turn output length, and task turnaround time** rather than public benchmark scores detached from everyday work. - **Inference**: Combining megakernels, 4-bit quantization, and [DFly2](#dfly2-for-speculative-decoding) pushes decoding speed past **150 tokens/s**, enabling low-cost serving at scale. ### Task Performance and Cost **Hy4 flash delivers overall task performance slightly above Hy4 preview at a much lower cost per task.** On WorkIndex, it scores **42.1**, compared with **39.7** for Hy4 preview, while its average cost per task is just **1/13 of Hy4 preview**, **1/20 of Hy4**, and **1/8 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017** (Max tier, peak-hour pricing).

Figure 1: Performance and cost across internal and external tasks. WorkIndex (internal) comprises 8 evaluation sets covering slide creation, slide editing, human-AI slide co-writing, Markdown human-AI co-writing, document editing, spreadsheet repair, audio/video processing, and visual understanding.
Open Benchmarks includes 7 public agent benchmarks: DeepSWE, ProgramBench, Terminal-Bench 4.0, APEX-Agents, AutomationBench, HLE, and OSWorld 2.1.

Figure 2: Average cost per task on WorkIndex. Task scores are 42.1 for Hy4 flash, 39.7 for Hy4 preview, and 51.4 for Hy4.

We recommend Hy4 flash for most everyday productivity tasks, including **deep search, document processing, slide creation, simple frontend demos, and computer use**. For complex tasks such as long-horizon software engineering, we recommend Hy4 for its higher intelligence ceiling. ### User Blind Evaluation In the blind evaluation, **Hy4 flash achieved user satisfaction close to Claude Haiku 5.5, while recording the lowest cost per task and shortest median end-to-end completion time among the evaluated models**. Its user satisfaction score was **2.79/4** (Claude Haiku 5.5: **2.81/4**), with a median end-to-end completion time of **6.7 minutes** and a cost of **RMB 0.26 per task**.

Figure 3: Blind evaluation with 85 internal WorkBuddy users across 259 tasks spanning 27 categories.

## Appendix: Benchmark results

## News * We release **Hy4 flash**, **Hy4 flash-FP8**, and the pre-trained **Hy4 flash-base** as open-weight models on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash), [ModelScope](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy4-flash), and [AtomGit](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy4-flash). ## Model Links | Model Name | Description | Hugging Face | ModelScope | AtomGit | |:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Hy4 flash | Instruct model | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash) | [Model](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy4-flash) | [Model](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy4-flash) | | Hy4 flash-FP8 | FP8 quantized instruct model | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash-FP8) | [Model](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy4-flash-FP8) | [Model](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy4-flash-FP8) | | Hy4 flash-base | Pre-trained base model | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash-base) | [Model](https://modelscope.cn/models/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy4-flash-base) | [Model](https://ai.gitcode.com/tencent_hunyuan/Hy4-flash-base) | Hy4 flash-base is a pre-trained base model, not an instruction-tuned chat model. The chat and reasoning examples below apply to Hy4 flash and Hy4 flash-FP8. ## Quickstart Use [Transformers](#transformers) to load the model for local inference, or deploy a server and access it through the [OpenAI-compatible API](#openai-compatible-api). > **Reasoning mode (instruct models)**: `reasoning_effort` supports `"high"` (default, thinking enabled) and `"no_think"` (direct responses). Both examples below use `"no_think"`. > > **Recommended sampling parameters**: `temperature=0.9`, `top_p=1.0`. ### Transformers > Support for Hy4 flash will be merged into the `transformers` main branch soon. Until then, install from the commit below. ```bash pip install "transformers[torch,vision] @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50903/head" ``` The following example generates a brief image description: ```python from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "tencent/Hy4-flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "image", "url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/pipeline-cat-chonk.jpeg", }, {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image in one sentence."}, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", reasoning_effort="no_think", ).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) print(processor.decode(outputs[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` ### OpenAI-compatible API For API access, start a server using the [vLLM deployment instructions](#vllm), then run the following client example: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") response = client.chat.completions.create( model="hy4-flash", messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Hello! Can you briefly introduce yourself?"}, ], temperature=0.9, top_p=1.0, extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "no_think"}}, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` ## Deployment ### DFly2 for Speculative Decoding DFly2 is Hy4 flash's speculative-decoding drafter, trained with [AngelSpec](https://github.com/Tencent/AngelSpec) and built directly on the target model's **Top-k Sparse KV**: each draft layer shares the KV cache (**KV Share**) and the compressed indexer's selection of up to 2,048 positions (**Index Share**) with its corresponding sparse attention layer. This yields three advantages: - **Constant cost**: each draft token attends to at most ~2K keys, regardless of context length. - **Zero extra KV memory**: no separate KV cache is maintained for the drafter. - **PD-disaggregation ready**: not involved in prefill; the prefill-to-decode transfer adds only one last-layer hidden state.

### Quantization We provide [AngelSlim](https://github.com/tencent/AngelSlim), a more accessible, comprehensive, and efficient toolkit for large model compression. AngelSlim supports a comprehensive suite of compression tools for large-scale multimodal models, including common quantization algorithms, low-bit quantization, and speculative sampling. For this model, we have provided a [GGUF](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Hy4-flash-GGUF) compressed version for end-to-end testing purposes. ### Inference Frameworks For production serving, we recommend using [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) or [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/). Please refer to the recipes: - [Hy4 flash vLLM Recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/tencent/Hy4-flash) - [Hy4 flash SGLang Cookbook](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Tencent/Hy4-flash) #### vLLM Use official prebuilt image `vllm/vllm-openai:hy4-flash`: ```bash docker run --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ --ipc=host \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:hy4-flash tencent/Hy4-flash-FP8 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --speculative-config '{"num_speculative_tokens":5,"method":"dfly"}' \ --attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE \ --tool-call-parser hy_v4 \ --reasoning-parser hy_v4 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 \ --served-model-name hy4-flash ``` #### SGLang Use the official prebuilt image `lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-flash` (multi-arch, x86 and Arm): ```bash docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-flash docker run --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ --ipc=host \ lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-flash \ sglang serve \ --trust-remote-code \ --model-path tencent/Hy4-flash-FP8 \ --tp 8 \ --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled \ --speculative-algorithm DFLY \ --speculative-dfly-block-size 6 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 ``` ## Finetuning Hy4 flash provides a complete model finetuning pipeline. For detailed documentation, please refer to: [Finetuning Guide](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash/blob/main/finetune/README.md) ## License Hy4 flash is released under the **Tencent Hy License**. See [LICENSE](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-flash/blob/main/LICENSE) for details. ## Contact Us If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to reach out to our R&D and product teams via email: 📧 **hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com** ---

--- license: apache-2.0 license_link: https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0 pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - conversational - image-text-to-text - moe library_name: transformers --- # Inkling 2 Mini

Playground | Tinker Cookbook

## 1. General Information Inkling 2 Mini is a general-purpose multimodal model that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is intended for use in English and other languages, and across multiple coding languages. The model is designed to be used by developers building AI-powered applications, including agentic and tool-use systems, coding assistants, chatbots, and retrieval-augmented generation systems, and is suitable for general-purpose conversational use, instruction-following, and other natural language and visual tasks. It is released with open weights to support research, fine-tuning and integration into third-party products by downstream developers. **Languages:** English, general multilingual support **Model provider:** Thinking Machines Lab, Inc. **Date of release:** November 20, 2026 **License:** Apache 2.0 [Model Acceptable Use Policy](https://thinkingmachines.ai/model-acceptable-use-policy/) ## 2. Getting Started The weights are available for download through Hugging Face [here](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini). Developers can also access the model using the Tinker fine-tuning platform, which provides API access. * For accessing our model via Tinker, you can get started by referring to the Tinker Cookbook [here](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/tinker-cookbook), and installing the tml-renderers package [here](https://pypi.org/project/tml-renderers/). * Tinker playground also provides inference-only access to the model [here](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground). ### Required hardware The model is distributed as a single checkpoint of about 20GB, in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 precisions. Given its small size, it is possible to run this checkpoint on local AI compute for inference. We support: * 1x NVIDIA DGX Spark * Apple silicon devices with 32GB or more memory (MacBooks, Mac minis and Studios) * Other GPUs and platforms are possible, with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended ### Required software Inkling 2 Mini supports inference using the following frameworks, along with their dependency libraries: * [Hugging Face](https://hf.co/blog/inkling2mini) * [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/ThinkingMachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [vLLM](https://recipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [TokenSpeed](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#inkling-2-mini) * NVIDIA Dynamo * [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/inkling-2-mini), including quantized GGUF versions * llama.cpp, for quantized GGUF versions * [Llama App](https://llama.app/) On Apple Silicon * [Ollama](https://ollama.com/library/inkling-2-mini) and Exo Labs Inkling 2 Mini can also be post-trained with: * [Miles](https://miles.radixark.com/docs/models/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini) * [SkyRL](https://docs.skyrl.ai/docs/models/inkling2) ## 3. Model Properties ### Model type Multimodal autoregressive looped transformer ### Architecture type A 24-layer decoder-only transformer with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layers. The middle 12 layers run three times with shared weights, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. In each layer, each token is routed to 8 of 128 experts. Attention is a hybrid of local and global layers. The model is natively multimodal – images are encoded via a vision transformer – with image and text inputs projected into a shared hidden space and processed jointly by the decoder. ### Parameters 26.4B, 3.4B active Note: each extra pass through the looped layers adds about 1.0B effective active parameters. Since the model runs with three passes, there are 5.4B effective active parameters per token. ### Numerics support NVFP4 and MXFP8 ### Input modalities * Text: UTF-8 encoded text * Image: Any pixel-based image input. For optimal performance, each image dimension should be between 40px to 4096px. Inkling 2 Mini supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. ### Output modalities Text ## 4. Training Training data includes a broad variety of content types, including text, images, video. Training data for the model was drawn from publicly available sources, acquired from third-parties, generated internally, or synthetically generated or augmented. Publicly available data includes content from the public internet and publicly accessible repositories. Data curation includes cleaning, processing, and modifying datasets. These processing steps, which vary by data type, may include deduplication and filtering to remove junk or other low-quality data, or to advance safety or other objectives. ## 5. Evaluations

## 6. Safety We conducted safety evaluations ahead of release, spanning both everyday human-AI interaction and dangerous-capability testing. Because Inkling 2 Mini is multimodal, we paid attention to whether safety behavior held consistently across text and image inputs. We applied mitigations to reduce risks before release, including an extra phase of alignment training using on-policy distillation, similarly to Inkling 2 Small. For everyday use, we evaluated sycophancy and how the model handles requests involving suicide, self-harm and eating disorders, including whether it encourages harm or affirms false beliefs. We also assessed whether the model refuses genuinely harmful requests without over-refusing benign ones. For CBRN and cyber, we assessed knowledge and procedural uplift through internal evaluations and refusal-suppressed variants intended to estimate latent capability with safeguards removed. For loss of control, we evaluated agentic capability, strategic deception, and sabotage potential, benchmarked against public frontier models, and found the model materially below frontier capabilities. Inkling 2 Mini is the first looped transformer we have released, so we also studied how looping affects monitorability: whether we can still oversee the model by reading its chain of thought. Looping lets the model do more computation without reasoning in visible tokens. Inkling 2 Mini has very little controllability over its chain of thought, and was unable to perform covert side tasks in realistic agentic environments. Further experiments on the effect of looping on monitorability are described in our [blog post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/). Across all areas, we concluded that Inkling 2 Mini does not give material uplift beyond what is already available from open-weights models. ## 7. Bias, risks and limitations Inkling 2 Mini may exhibit general limitations common to foundation models, including hallucination (generating plausible but factually incorrect or unsupported content), occasional failures to follow instructions precisely, and degraded performance in long multi-turn conversations. As with other models trained on web-derived and synthetic data, it may reflect biases present in its training data, including demographic, cultural or linguistic biases, and may perform unevenly across languages, dialects or subject domains that were less represented during training. Inkling 2 Mini’s knowledge is limited to information available as of its training cutoff, and it may not reflect events or changes that occurred afterward. Inkling 2 Mini is a small model built to run on local hardware, and some limitations are specific to it: * Knowledge and factual accuracy. It is less capable than Inkling 2 Small across most of our evaluations, with the largest gaps on factual recall and knowledge-heavy questions. It is more likely than larger models to state incorrect information with confidence. * Repetitive reasoning. In internal testing the model sometimes became stuck in long reasoning loops, or repeatedly re-checked its own work without making progress, particularly when debugging code. We recommend setting limits on output tokens and agent turns. * Agentic reliability. When using tools, it is less reliable than larger models at following detailed instructions and project conventions. It may take destructive actions, such as deleting or overwriting files, without confirmation, and may not report the outcome of its work accurately. * Languages other than English. Output quality can be lower outside English. In testing in Chinese we observed clipped phrasing and mixed languages. * Sensitive topics. The model can respond with more caution than the situation calls for when a conversation touches on mental health. * Reasoning and compute. Setting reasoning effort to its minimum does not fully disable reasoning. Because the middle layers run three times, compute per token is higher than the active-parameter count alone suggests. * Local performance. Support for looped models in local runtimes is new, and speed varies by runtime and hardware. We recommend that downstream developers and deployers: * Apply appropriate human oversight and review for outputs used in high-stakes or safety-critical contexts, rather than relying on Inkling 2 Mini’s outputs without verification. * Run agentic workloads in a sandbox, and require confirmation before destructive or irreversible actions. * Conduct their own evaluation of Inkling 2 Mini’s performance, safety and fairness for their specific use case, language and population prior to deployment, particularly for applications involving vulnerable groups. * Implement additional safeguards, such as content filtering, rate limiting and monitoring, at the application layer, especially for open deployment contexts where Inkling 2 Mini’s built-in mitigations may not be sufficient on their own. * Avoid deploying Inkling 2 Mini in domains such as medical, legal or safety-critical decision-making without additional fine-tuning, domain-specific validation and human oversight. ## 8. --- license: apache-2.0 license_link: https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0 pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - conversational - image-text-to-text - moe library_name: transformers --- # Inkling 2 Small

NVFP4 | MXFP8 | Playground | Tinker Cookbook | Acceptable Use

## 1. General Information Inkling 2 Small is a general-purpose multimodal model that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is intended for use in English and other languages, and across multiple coding languages. The model is designed to be used by developers building AI-powered applications, including agentic and tool-use systems, coding assistants, chatbots, and retrieval-augmented generation systems, and is suitable for general-purpose conversational use, instruction-following, and other natural language and visual tasks. It is released with open weights to support research, fine-tuning and integration into third-party products by downstream developers. **Languages:** English, with general multilingual capabilities across other languages. ## 2. Getting Started Try Inkling 2 Small on the [Tinker Playground](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground) or access via API using the [Tinker Cookbook](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/tinker-cookbook). To fine-tune Inkling 2 Small with Tinker, also install the [tml-renderers](https://pypi.org/project/tml-renderers/) package. Inkling 2 Small supports local inference using: * SGLang ([recipe](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/ThinkingMachines/Inkling-2-Small)) * vLLM ([recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small)) * TokenSpeed ([recipe](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#inkling-2)) * Unsloth ([recipe](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/inkling-2)) Inkling 2 Small can also be post-trained with: * [Miles](https://miles.radixark.com/docs/models/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-small) * [SkyRL](https://docs.skyrl.ai/docs/models/inkling2) * [Snowflake Cortex Training](https://github.com/snowflakedb/cortex-training) API access is also available through third party inference providers, including: * NVIDIA * Fireworks * [Together](https://www.together.ai/models/inkling-2-small) * [Baseten](https://www.baseten.co/library/inkling-2-small) * [Nebius](https://tokenfactory.nebius.com/endpoints/public/thinkingmachines%2FInkling-2-Small) * [Modal](https://modal.com/library/thinking-machines/inkling-2-small) * [Cloudflare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/inkling-2-small/) ### Required hardware The model is distributed in two checkpoint formats. The main NVFP4 checkpoint requires a GPU cluster with at least 500GB of aggregated VRAM. This can be met with either of the following example configurations: * 2x NVIDIA B300 GPUs * 4x NVIDIA H200 GPUs The alternative MXFP8 checkpoint requires a GPU cluster with at least 800GB of aggregated VRAM. This can be met with either of the following example configurations: * 4x NVIDIA B300 GPUs * 8x NVIDIA H200 GPUs The model was pretrained, midtrained and post-trained in NVFP4, so this is the native precision for the model. We recommend the NVFP4 checkpoint for all use-cases, and we're confident that it's the best option. The MXFP8 has a very marginal 1–2 percentage points gain over the NVFP4 checkpoint over evals, but we do not think it is meaningful for any practical use-cases. ### Required software Running the model directly on GPU hardware requires an inference deployment framework — either SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed, Unsloth, or Hugging Face, along with all of their respective dependency libraries. ## 3. Model Properties ### Model type Multimodal autoregressive transformer ### Architecture type A 48-layer decoder-only transformer with a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward backbone: each token is routed to 8 of 384 experts. Attention is a hybrid of local and global layers. The model is natively multimodal — images are encoded via a vision transformer — with image and text inputs projected into a shared hidden space and processed jointly by the decoder. ### Parameters 594B total, 17B active ### Numerics support MXFP8 and NVFP4 ### Input modalities Inkling 2 Small accepts text input in UTF-8 encoding and image input in any pixel-based format (with each dimension ideally between 40px and 4096px for optimal performance). It supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. ### Output modalities Inkling 2 Small generates output as UTF-8 encoded text. ## 4. Training Training data includes a broad variety of content types, including text, images, video. Training data for the model was drawn from publicly available sources, acquired from third-parties, generated internally, or synthetically generated or augmented. Publicly available data includes content from the public internet and publicly accessible repositories. The training data curation process includes cleaning, processing, and modifying datasets. These processing steps, which vary by data type, may include deduplication and filtering to remove junk or other low-quality data, or to advance safety or other objectives. ## 5. Evaluations

It is released with open weights to support research, fine-tuning and integration into third-party products by downstream developers. **Languages:** English, with general multilingual capabilities across other languages. ## 2. Getting Started Try Inkling-Small on the [Tinker Playground](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground) or access via API using the [Tinker Cookbook](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/tinker-cookbook). Inkling-Small supports local deployment using the following open-source libraries: * SGLang ([recipe](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/ThinkingMachines/Inkling-Small)) * vLLM ([recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small)) * TokenSpeed ([recipe](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#Inkling)) * Unsloth ([recipe](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/inkling)) * Huggingface ([recipe](https://hf.co/blog/thinkingmachines-inkling)) API access is also available through third party inference providers. ## 3. Model Properties ### Model type Multimodal autoregressive transformer ### Architecture type A 42-layer decoder-only transformer with a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward backbone: each token is routed to 6 of 256 experts, plus 2 shared experts active on every token. Attention is a hybrid of local and global layers. The model is natively multimodal — images are encoded via a hierarchical patch encoder, and audio via discrete token encoding — with all modalities projected into a shared hidden space and processed jointly by the decoder. ### Parameters 276B total, 12B active ### Numerics support BF16 and NVFP4 ### Input modalities Inkling-Small accepts text, image, and audio inputs: - Text: UTF-8 encoded text - Image: Any pixel-based image input. For optimal performance, each image dimension should be between 40px to 4096px. - Audio: WAV format, sampled at 16kHz. For optimal performance, audio length should ideally be under 2 mins. ### Output modalities Inkling-Small generates output as UTF-8 encoded text. ## 4. Training Training data includes a broad variety of content types, including text, images, audio, video. Training data for the model was drawn from publicly available sources, acquired from third-parties, or synthetically generated or augmented. Publicly available data includes content from the public internet and publicly accessible repositories. The training data curation process includes cleaning, processing, and modifying datasets. These processing steps, which vary by data type, may include deduplication and filtering to remove junk or other low-quality data, or to advance safety or other objectives. ## 5. Evaluations

Otherwise, we report performance using our internal harness. - Audio MC: Other models were evaluated internally since they are not on the official leaderboard. - VoiceBench: VoiceBench uses rule-based, hard-coded string matching for grading, making the evaluation sensitive to output-formatting differences. We therefore added a system message instructing models to follow the expected answer format. - HLE with tools: We benchmarked Minimax M2.7, Claude 4.5 Haiku, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and GPT 5.6 Luna using our internal harness. ## 6. Safety We conducted safety evaluations ahead of release, spanning both everyday human-AI interaction and dangerous-capability testing. Because Inkling-Small is multimodal, we paid attention to whether safety behavior held consistently across text, audio, and image inputs. We applied mitigations to reduce risks before release. For everyday interaction, we evaluated sycophancy, harmful manipulation, and psychological-harm patterns like parasocial dependency and validation of delusional reasoning, including through multi-turn, open-ended external red-teaming designed to surface issues that only emerge over longer conversations. We also assessed whether the model refuses genuinely harmful requests without over-refusing benign ones. For CBRN and cyber, we assessed knowledge and procedural uplift through internal evaluations, external testing, and refusal-suppressed variants intended to estimate latent capability with safeguards removed. For loss of control, we evaluated agentic capability, strategic deception, and sabotage potential, benchmarked against public frontier models, and found the model materially below frontier capabilities. Across all areas, we concluded that Inkling-Small did not present risk of material uplift beyond what's already available in the open-weight ecosystem. The residual risks identified in our evaluations — specifically, Inkling-Small’s occasional tendency to comply with role-play and indirectly framed prompts concerning harmful topics — are consistent with what you would see from any open-weight model, and are best addressed with defense-in-depth rather than relying on the model's refusals alone. Common downstream moderation tools, such as Llama Guard, are compatible with Inkling-Small and can be layered around the model to catch jailbreak attempts, filter unsafe outputs, and enforce use-case-specific policies. We would encourage treating this kind of input/output classification as a part of your deployment stack, especially for consumer-facing or high-traffic applications where adversarial prompting is more likely. ## 7. Bias, risks and limitations Inkling-Small may exhibit general limitations common to foundation models, including hallucination (generating plausible but factually incorrect or unsupported content), occasional failures to follow instructions precisely, and degraded performance in long multi-turn conversations. As with other large-scale models trained on web-derived and synthetic data, Inkling-Small may reflect biases present in its training data, including demographic, cultural, or linguistic biases, and may perform unevenly across languages, dialects, or subject domains that were less represented during training. Inkling-Small's knowledge is limited to information available as of its training cutoff, and it may not reflect events, developments, or changes that occurred afterward. We recommend that downstream developers and deployers apply appropriate human oversight and review for outputs used in high-stakes or safety-critical contexts, rather than relying on Inkling-Small's outputs without verification. - Conduct their own evaluation of Inkling-Small's performance, safety, and fairness for their specific use case, language, and population prior to deployment, particularly for applications involving vulnerable groups. - Implement additional safeguards – such as content filtering, rate limiting, and monitoring – at the application layer, especially for open deployment contexts where Inkling-Small's built-in mitigations may not be sufficient on their own. - Avoid deploying Inkling-Small in domains such as medical, legal, or safety-critical decision-making without additional fine-tuning, domain-specific validation, and human oversight ## 8. # L0xRE-V2-27b-Low

**A capable 27B agent on a 12 GB GPU. 256K context with sparse attention, the same size and speed as L0xRE-27b-Low, and closer to the full model.**

L0xRE-V2-27b-Low is the second-generation weight set for L0xRE Low, a quantized Qwen3.8-27B derivative for local coding assistants and AI agents. The file size is unchanged (**8.62 GB**, every layer on the GPU), as is the speed. V2 is a refit with better calibration and a re-balanced mix of 2-bit and 3-bit codes, and it is measurably closer to the BF16 model, especially on code, tool calls and agent traces.

> **Runtime: L0xRE v0.1.6.5 (Sparse Defaults) or later.** This is the default model for the sparse runtime. The [repository home page](https://github.com/seanyourhighness/L0xRE-BeeLLama-Low) always names the current release and the install/update steps, so start there rather than at a pinned release. Runtime updates do not change the weights in this repository.

## Sparse attention and 256K context

v0.1.6 made sparse attention the default above 8K tokens and raised the 12 GB profile to **262,144 tokens**. v0.1.6.5 promotes the current defaults. The same 12 GB card now serves twice the context, with retrieval close to dense in the measured tests.

- **Below 8K tokens:** fully dense. Outputs are logit-identical to the dense path, not merely close.
- **Above 8K tokens:** each query attends to a sink, a local window, and the most relevant earlier tokens selected by a learned D-LSA map (`qwen38-dlsa-d2048.l0xmap`, installed next to the model). v0.1.6.5 defaults are 256-token tiles, top-k 16,384, an 11,648-token sink, pooled prefill, a generation anchor, and CLOCK unit-cache gather v3.
- **Exact-match retrieval links:** a rare token sequence seen earlier hard-links the current block back to those earlier blocks. This targets the main failure of learned sparse attention, picking the wrong one of several similar records. Generation uses the plain sparse selection, so decode speed is unchanged.
- **Dense fallback:** `L0XRE_SPARSE=0` disables sparse attention. Dense mode is not the default above 8K; it mis-handles some agent transcripts past about 30K tokens.

### Measured sparse quality

These are the v0.1.6 release measurements with L0xRE-V2-27b-Low + DFlash2 at temperature 0:

| Test | Dense | v0.1.6 sparse |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Needle recall, 8 records in real agent transcripts, 16K–192K (RTX 3060 and RTX 5090) | 224/224 on each card | 223/224 on each card |
| Held-out retrieval (code, paths, paraphrased questions), two prompt sets, RTX 5090 | 269/288 | 268/288 |
| Responses below 8K tokens | — | bit-identical to the dense path (logit hashes) |
| Prefill cost, same runtime without the links | — | RTX 3060 −0.2…+0.1%; RTX 4090 −0.4…−0.1%; RTX 5090 within 1.6% |

v0.1.6.5's lab quality run (F1 + DFlash2 + s2 template) measured KL versus dense on real Hermes trajectories at **0.0107** for 42–78K, **0.0140** for 128–170K, and **0.0263** for 180–200K, with recall **72/72**, matching dense. This is an internal lab result, not an external leaderboard.

Known limits: one sequence at a time (`-np 1`); exact-match links can copy a neighbour at counting positions (for example a chapter number after "CHAPTER"); confident disagreements with dense attention remain at the plain-sparse rate of **1 in 862 positions**; tree verify runs inside the resident window up to 8K, and deeper verify uses the 8-row chain.

## What improved

KLD against BF16 Qwen3.8-27B, on gen-masked positions of the public [quant-challenge golden set](https://huggingface.co/datasets/StillDeadcode/qwen3.8-27b-quant-challenge). Lower is better. **Holdout** is 200 documents frozen before any fitting and scored once, for this release.

| Split | L0xRE-27b-Low (v1) | L0xRE-V2-27b-Low | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Holdout, 200 docs: overall | 0.1223 | **0.0928** | **−24.2%** [−20.4, −26.9] |
| Holdout: agentic mean (code, tools, reasoning, math) | 0.0701 | **0.0497** | **−29.1%** |
| Holdout: code | 0.0752 | **0.0499** | **−33.7%** |
| Holdout: agent and SWE traces | 0.0596 | **0.0383** | **−35.8%** |
| Development, 116 docs: overall | 0.1151 | **0.0833** | **−27.7%** |

V2 has lower KLD on 190 of the 200 holdout documents. Its weakest case is a thinking-off prompt that keeps the xhigh reasoning instruction with an empty think block, where a few chat and tool documents score worse. v0.1.5's thinking-off serving mode does not render that prompt.

## Benchmarks

Club-3090 8-pack N150 (150 tasks: tool calls, instruction following, structured output, data extraction, reasoning/math, bug finding, Hermes agent and CLI tasks):

| Mode | v1 (B02-A2 weights) | **V2** |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Thinking off, RTX 3060 | 119 | **121** |
| Thinking on, medium effort, 8K reasoning budget, ×2 (pass@1 / pass@3) | — | **127/133, 125/135** |

For comparison, v1 scored 127/133 with thinking on at **xhigh** effort and no reasoning budget, which took about twice as long per run.

## Speed

RTX 3060 12 GB, native Linux, headless, DFlash2 drafter, `bench.sh`. Paired against v1 weights on the same build and flags:

| Metric | V2 | Versus v1 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Narrative decode | ~45 tok/s | within 2% |
| Code decode | ~78 tok/s | within 2% |
| 10K prompt prefill | ~720 tok/s | within 1% |
| 90K prompt prefill | ~480 tok/s | within 1% |
| Decode at 90K depth (3 runs each) | 61.3 tok/s | v1 50.2 |

Decode at depth depends mostly on how many tokens the drafter gets accepted, so single runs vary widely. The per-step compute cost is the same for both weight sets.

### v0.1.6.5 sparse runtime check

On the same RTX 3060 12 GB, the v0.1.6.5 release kit booted at **11,175 MiB / 12,288 MiB** with the full 262,144-token sparse context and Q8_0 vision. `bench.sh` measured **55.73 tok/s** narrative (transformer essay) and **100.17 tok/s** code (Python quicksort), with **839 tok/s** prefill at 10K and **688 tok/s** prefill at 90K. These use the v0.1.6.5 sparse defaults and are not directly comparable with the paired agent-prompt table above.

## Model files

| File | Purpose | Size |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `L0xRE-V2-27b-Low.gguf` | Main model, sha256 `8eb326fddc73abae8ab26ae1c33fdeafd9d773c2702836a9fed77339bc537459` | 8.62 GB |
| `Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-Q4_K_M.gguf` | Recommended DFlash2 drafter (unchanged from v1), sha256 `1a25c56858e1ebe93f2718ac1d49d1151f9323325c1bbfd6209370f4db131ebd` | 1.14 GB |
| `qwen38-dlsa-d2048.l0xmap` | D-LSA sparse-attention map installed next to the model (v0.1.6+) | 6 MB |

**This model requires the [L0xRE BeeLLama Low runtime](https://github.com/seanyourhighness/L0xRE-BeeLLama-Low), v0.1.5 or later. The current v0.1.6.5 release adds the sparse defaults described above.** The API model name is still `L0xRE-27b-Low`, so existing client settings keep working. Stock llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Transformers and other engines are not supported. The GGUF extension alone does not mean it is compatible.

# Laguna S 2.1 Laguna S 2.1 is a 118B total parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 8B activated parameters per token, designed for agentic coding and long-horizon work. It sits between [Laguna XS 2.1](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-XS-2.1) (33B-A3B) and Laguna M.1 (225B-A23B) in the Laguna series and shares the family recipe: a token-choice router with softplus gating over 256 routed experts plus one shared expert, grouped-query attention, and interleaved full/sliding-window attention. >[!NOTE] >Laguna S 2.1 is released under OpenMDW-1.1, a fully permissive license. Use it, modify it, and build commercial products on it. No permission required. If you want more than the weights: production support, latency and cost optimization, or output indemnification, [talk to us](https://poolside.ai/contact?utm_source=hf&utm_medium=modelcard_cta). ## Highlights - **Mixed SWA and global attention layout**: 48 layers in a 1:3 global-to-SWA ratio (12 global attention layers, 36 sliding-window layers, window 512), with softplus attention gating and per-layer-type rotary scales - **1M context**: 1,048,576-token context window - **Native reasoning support**: interleaved thinking between tool calls, with per-request control via `enable_thinking` - **Speculative decoding**: a trained [DFlash draft model](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-DFlash) is available for lower-latency serving - **Quantized variants**: [FP8](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-FP8), [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-NVFP4), [INT4](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-INT4) and [GGUF](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-GGUF) - **OpenMDW-1.1 license**: Use and modify the model and associated materials freely for commercial and non-commercial purposes ([learn more about OpenMDW](https://openmdw.ai/)) ## Model overview - Number of parameters: 118B total, ~8B activated per token - Layers: 48 (12 global attention, 36 sliding-window attention) - Experts: 256 routed (top-10) plus 1 shared expert - Attention: grouped-query, 8 KV heads, head dim 128; per-head softplus output gating - Sliding window: 512 tokens - Context window: 1,048,576 tokens - Vocabulary: 100,352 tokens (Laguna family tokenizer) - Modality: text-to-text - Reasoning: interleaved thinking with preserved thinking ## Benchmark results

| Model | Size | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | SWE-bench Multilingual | SWE-Bench Pro (Public Dataset) | DeepSWE | SWE Atlas (Codebase QnA) | Toolathlon Verified | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Laguna S 2.1** | 118B-A8B | **70.2%** | **78.5%** | **59.4%** | **40.4%** | **46.2%** | **49.7%** | | Tencent Hy3 | 295B-A21B | 71.7% | 75.8% | 57.9% | - | - | - | | Inkling | 975B-A41B | 63.8% | - | 54.3% | - | - | 45.5%* | | Nemotron 3 Ultra | 550B-A55B | 56.4% | 67.7% | - | - | - | 34.3%* | | DeepSeek-V4-Pro Max | 1.6T-A49B | 64.0%* | 76.2% | 55.4% | 9.0%* | 27.2%* | 55.9%* | | Kimi K3 | 2800B-A50B | 88.3% | - | - | 69% | - | - | | Qwen 3.7 Max | - | 74.5%* | 78.3% | 60.6% | - | - | - | | Muse Spark 1.1 | - | 80% | - | 61.5% | 53.3% | 42.2%* | 75.6% | | Claude Fable 5 | - | 88% | - | 80.3% | 70% | - | - | Benchmarks as of 21 July 2026. Laguna S 2.1 in **bold**; a dash (-) marks a benchmark a model was not evaluated on. Scores marked * are as reported by third parties: Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE via Artificial Analysis, SWE Atlas via Scale AI's official leaderboard, and Toolathlon Verified via its official leaderboard. Full evaluation trajectories: [trajectories.poolside.ai](https://trajectories.poolside.ai). ## Usage Laguna S 2.1 uses the same `laguna` architecture as Laguna XS 2.1, so the same engine integrations apply (vLLM, SGLang, Transformers, TRT-LLM, llama.cpp). At 118B parameters the BF16 checkpoint needs multiple GPUs (roughly 236GB of weights); quantized variants reduce this substantially. ### vLLM ```shell vllm serve \ --model poolside/Laguna-S-2.1 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tool-call-parser poolside_v1 \ --reasoning-parser poolside_v1 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --served-model-name laguna \ --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": true}' ``` > [!NOTE] > **Optional: speculative decoding with DFlash.** Pair with the > [Laguna S 2.1 DFlash draft model](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-DFlash) > by adding > `--speculative-config '{"model":"poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-DFlash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"method":"dflash"}'`. ### SGLang ```shell python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path poolside/Laguna-S-2.1 \ --tp-size 4 \ --reasoning-parser poolside_v1 \ --tool-call-parser poolside_v1 \ --trust-remote-code ``` ### TRT-LLM ```shell trtllm-serve poolside/Laguna-S-2.1 --trust-remote-code \ --tool_parser poolside_v1 --reasoning_parser laguna ``` Note the flag names differ from vLLM's (`--tool_parser`, and the reasoning parser is `laguna`, not `poolside_v1`). ### llama.cpp GGUF conversions are available at [poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-GGUF). Serve with poolside's llama.cpp fork, branch [`laguna`](https://github.com/poolsideai/llama.cpp/tree/laguna), which carries full Laguna support including DFlash speculative decoding. (Base Laguna support is also in upstream review: [ggml-org/llama.cpp#25165](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25165).) ```shell git clone --branch laguna https://github.com/poolsideai/llama.cpp cd llama.cpp && cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j ./build/bin/llama-server -m laguna-s-2.1-Q4_K_M.gguf --jinja --port 8000 # with DFlash speculative decoding: ./build/bin/llama-server -m laguna-s-2.1-Q4_K_M.gguf \ -md laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf \ --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 7 -fa on --jinja --port 8000 ``` ### Ollama Run directly from the [Ollama library](https://ollama.com/library/laguna-s-2.1): ```shell ollama run laguna-s-2.1 ``` Quantization variants are available as tags (`q4_K_M`, `q8_0`, `f16`, `mxfp8`, `nvfp4`, `mlx-bf16`), for example `ollama run laguna-s-2.1:q8_0`. The Laguna chat template is baked into the model, so tool-calling and interleaved reasoning work automatically. ## Controlling reasoning Laguna S 2.1 has native reasoning support and works best with *preserved thinking*: keep `reasoning_content` from prior assistant messages in the message history. The model will generally reason before calling tools and between tool calls, and may stop reasoning in follow-up steps if prior thinking blocks are dropped. Thinking is controlled per request via the chat template: ```python extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}} ``` or at the server level with `--default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": true}'`.
